title: The return of the hunters
sub: Europe's experiment with large predators is testing the limits of ecological ambition and rural patience

paras.x: The term 'rewilding' was coined in the early 1990s by American conservationists who argued that protecting isolated fragments of habitat was no longer enough. Their prescription, summarised in the shorthand 'cores, corridors and carnivores', called for large connected reserves in which top predators could once again regulate the ecosystems beneath them. When the idea crossed the Atlantic, it was quietly reshaped. Europe has few true wilderness areas, and most of its land has been farmed, grazed or managed for centuries. European advocates therefore tended to speak less of restoring a pristine past and more of stepping back from intervention, allowing natural processes to resume wherever economic pressure had eased. The abandonment of marginal farmland across southern and eastern Europe since the 1960s, estimated at some 20 million hectares, gave the movement unexpected room in which to operate.

Perhaps the most striking evidence that large carnivores can live alongside dense human populations has come not from planned releases but from animals that returned of their own accord. Wolves, legally protected under the 1979 Bern Convention, dispersed from refuges in Italy and the Carpathian Mountains and recolonised Germany from 2000 onwards, where more than 180 packs are now thought to exist. A survey led by Dr Henrik Lindqvist of Uppsala University found that roughly a third of mainland Europe hosts at least one species of large carnivore, much of it outside national parks and nature reserves. Lindqvist's team concluded that the American model of keeping people and predators apart was neither available nor necessary on a continent where the two appeared able to share the same terrain, provided that hunting was controlled.

The ecological argument for predators rests largely on the notion of the trophic cascade, in which the influence of a carnivore ripples down through the food chain. The textbook case is Yellowstone National Park, where the reintroduction of wolves in 1995 was credited with reducing browsing by elk, allowing willow and aspen to recover along riverbanks and, in turn, stabilising the rivers themselves. This narrative, popularised by a widely shared online film, has since been qualified. Research by Dr Marion Keast at Colorado State University suggested that the decline in elk owed as much to human hunters, drought and a growing number of bears as to wolves, and that some streams had changed so much in the wolves' absence that their banks could not simply revert. Whether the crowded European countryside, criss-crossed by roads and fences, would display cascades at all remains uncertain.

Proposals to bring back the Eurasian lynx to Britain, where it disappeared around 1,300 years ago, illustrate how quickly the debate shifts from biology to social trust. The lynx is a secretive animal that preys mainly on roe deer and has no recorded history of attacking people, and modelling by conservation groups identified enough forest in Northumberland and the Scottish Highlands to support a viable population. Yet an application for a trial release was rejected after a consultation revealed widespread hostility among sheep farmers. Many objected less to the predicted losses, which were small, than to the sense that decisions about their land were being taken by urban organisations with little stake in the outcome. 'What people are defending is a way of life, not a handful of lambs,' observed the rural sociologist Dr Fiona Gilchrist of the University of Aberdeen.

Governments have usually attempted to buy acceptance through compensation. In France, the state spent roughly 30 million euros in a single recent year on livestock killed by wolves and on preventive measures such as electric fencing and guard dogs. Such schemes, however, have a mixed record. Payments are often delayed, and farmers must prove that a carcass was killed by a protected predator rather than by a stray dog, a requirement many find humiliating. Economists at Wageningen University have argued for a different approach in which herders are paid according to the number of predators breeding on their land, rewarding coexistence rather than reimbursing loss. A Swedish version of this, applied to wolverines in reindeer-herding areas since 1996, appears to have reduced illegal killing, although the evidence is drawn from a small number of districts.

The political mood has shifted noticeably in recent years. Following a series of well-publicised attacks on livestock, including one in which a pony belonging to a senior European official was killed, the standing committee of the Bern Convention voted in December 2024 to downgrade the wolf from 'strictly protected' to 'protected', making culling easier. Supporters of the change described it as a pragmatic recognition of the wolf's recovery; critics argued that it rewarded a lobby that had never accepted the animal's presence. Meanwhile, poaching remains common. One study of radio-collared wolves in Scandinavia estimated that half of all deaths were caused by illegal killing, and that around two-thirds of those were never detected, since the bodies and collars simply vanished.

For many ecologists, the lesson of the past three decades is that the future of Europe's predators will be decided less in forests than in village halls. Professor Arjen de Vries, who advises the Dutch government on wildlife policy, predicts that populations will continue to grow until roughly 2040 but that their distribution will increasingly reflect local tolerance rather than the quality of the habitat. He suggests that projects which involve farmers from the outset, sharing both decision-making and income from wildlife tourism, are more likely to endure than those imposed from above. If he is right, the wildest parts of the continent may turn out to be not the most remote, but the most willing.

title: The forgotten carbon vaults
sub: Peatlands cover a tiny share of the planet yet hold more carbon than all its forests. Can the damage be undone?

paras.x: Peat forms wherever plant material accumulates faster than it can decay, most commonly in waterlogged ground where a lack of oxygen slows the work of bacteria and fungi. The process is extraordinarily slow: a typical bog in northern Europe gains around a millimetre of depth a year, so a deposit five metres thick may represent five millennia of growth. Although peatlands occupy only about three per cent of the world's land surface, they are thought to contain some 600 billion tonnes of carbon, roughly twice the amount stored in the vegetation of all the world's forests. Most lie in the cold, wet regions of Canada, Russia and Scandinavia, but some of the deepest deposits are tropical, notably in Indonesia and in the Congo Basin, where a vast peat complex was mapped for the first time only in 2017.

For most of human history, peat was regarded not as a carbon store but as either a resource or an obstacle. In Ireland and the Netherlands it was cut and dried for fuel on an industrial scale; by the seventeenth century, Dutch cities depended on it to heat homes and power breweries. Elsewhere, bogs were drained to create farmland, a practice encouraged by government grants in Britain until the 1980s. More recently, demand has come from gardeners, since peat retains moisture and is free of weed seeds, making it an ideal growing medium. The cumulative effect has been severe. Dr Katrin Vogel of the University of Greifswald estimates that around 12 per cent of the world's peatlands have now been drained, and that these damaged areas release close to five per cent of all greenhouse gases produced by human activity.

The reason drainage is so harmful lies in the chemistry of decay. Once the water table falls, oxygen penetrates the upper layers and microbes begin breaking down organic matter that may have been preserved for thousands of years, releasing it as carbon dioxide. The ground itself sinks as a result, a phenomenon known as subsidence. In the Fens of eastern England, a cast-iron post driven into the peat in 1851 so that its top was level with the surface now protrudes by about four metres. Dried peat is also highly flammable. During the 2015 fires in Indonesia, which burned largely on drained plantation land, daily emissions for several weeks were estimated to exceed those of the entire United States economy. Such fires can smoulder underground for months, making them extremely difficult to extinguish.

Restoration, in principle, is simple: raise the water table again. In practice, it involves blocking thousands of kilometres of drainage ditches with dams made of peat, timber or plastic piling, and sometimes reprofiling the land so that water spreads evenly across it. On bare surfaces left by industrial extraction, conservationists may scatter fragments of sphagnum moss, the plant largely responsible for building northern bogs, to kick-start regrowth. The Flow Country of northern Scotland, where conifer plantations were established on deep peat in the 1980s with the help of tax incentives, has become something of a testing ground. There, teams have felled trees and filled in the furrows left by ploughing, and monitoring suggests that within a decade water levels on many sites have returned close to those of undisturbed bog.

Rewetting is not, however, an instant climate solution. Waterlogged peat produces methane, a gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide over short periods, and newly flooded sites can emit it in substantial quantities, particularly where fresh vegetation rots in the rising water. Some critics have used this to question the value of restoration altogether. Dr Lena Hartmann of the Leibniz Centre for Agricultural Research argues that this objection misreads the arithmetic. In her group's modelling, the methane released after rewetting is outweighed within a few decades by the carbon dioxide no longer escaping from the drained peat, and because methane breaks down in the atmosphere within about twelve years while carbon dioxide persists for centuries, the long-term benefit is clear. 'The worst option,' she says, 'is to leave a drained peatland as it is.'

The greater obstacle is economic. Much drained peat is now highly productive farmland: the Fens alone grow about a third of England's vegetables, and in Germany some seven per cent of agricultural land lies on drained peat. Raising water levels would end conventional cultivation there. One proposed compromise is paludiculture, the farming of wet peatland with crops adapted to saturated soil, such as reeds for thatching, cattails for insulation board, or water buffalo for meat. Trials in north-eastern Germany have shown such crops to be technically feasible, but markets for them remain small and farmers who adopt them face several years of reduced income. Without long-term public support, economists argue, few landowners will make the switch voluntarily.

Whether restoration can be scaled up may depend on finding a reliable way to pay for it. Carbon markets offer one possibility, and Britain's Peatland Code, launched in 2015, allows companies to buy credits that fund the rewetting of specific sites. Critics point out that measuring the carbon actually saved is difficult, since emissions vary with weather, vegetation and the depth of the water table from month to month. Satellite techniques that detect tiny changes in ground height, a sign of whether peat is growing or wasting away, may eventually make verification cheaper. For now, the scientists involved tend to be cautious. Professor Ian Rowe of the University of Leeds notes that protecting peat which is still intact costs a fraction of repairing what has been lost, a lesson he believes policymakers have been slow to absorb.

title: Chasing zero resistance
sub: For more than a century, physicists have hunted for a material that conducts electricity perfectly at everyday temperatures, with some famous successes and some notable embarrassments

paras.x: In April 1911, in a laboratory in Leiden, the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes and his assistants cooled a thread of mercury with liquid helium to about four degrees above absolute zero and watched its electrical resistance vanish. Nobody had predicted the effect, and for some time Onnes suspected a short circuit. What he had found was superconductivity: a state in which current flows without any loss of energy, so that a loop of superconducting wire can, in theory, carry a current indefinitely. A second defining property emerged in 1933, when German researchers showed that superconductors actively expel magnetic fields from their interior, which is why a small magnet can hover above one. These two features made the phenomenon one of the most coveted in physics, but for decades it remained confined to conditions colder than anything found naturally on Earth.

An explanation took almost half a century to arrive. In 1957 John Bardeen, Leon Cooper and Robert Schrieffer proposed that, below a critical temperature, electrons in certain metals form loosely bound pairs, held together by subtle vibrations in the crystal lattice. Paired in this way, they move through the material in a co-ordinated fashion and are no longer scattered by impurities, which is what normally causes resistance. The theory, known by its authors' initials as BCS, earned a Nobel Prize in 1972 and remains one of the great achievements of twentieth-century physics. It also appeared to set a ceiling. Because lattice vibrations are too weak to hold electron pairs together when atoms are jostling with heat, many theorists concluded that superconductivity could not survive much above 30 kelvin, or about minus 243 degrees Celsius.

That assumption was overturned in 1986, when Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller, working at IBM in Zurich, reported superconductivity at 35 kelvin in a ceramic compound of copper and oxygen, a class of material previously considered a poor conductor. Within a year, a related compound was found to superconduct at 92 kelvin, above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen, a coolant that costs roughly as much as milk rather than the expensive helium previously required. The announcement provoked such excitement that a session of the American Physical Society in New York in March 1987 ran until three in the morning and was nicknamed the 'Woodstock of physics'. Yet nearly four decades later, the mechanism behind these 'cuprate' superconductors is still not agreed upon, and the record for materials at normal pressure has barely moved since 1993.

The most dramatic advances since then have come from an unexpected direction. In 2015 a team at the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Mainz squeezed hydrogen sulphide between two diamonds at pressures more than a million times that of the atmosphere and recorded superconductivity at 203 kelvin. Lanthanum hydride later pushed the figure to about 250 kelvin, close to the temperature of a cold winter's day in Siberia. The rationale had been outlined decades earlier: hydrogen, the lightest element, vibrates at very high frequencies, which strengthens the pairing of electrons. The drawback is obvious. The samples are smaller than a grain of sand and exist only inside diamond anvils, so although they satisfy the physicist's definition of high-temperature superconductivity, they have no practical use whatsoever.

The field has also attracted claims that did not survive scrutiny. Physicists half-jokingly refer to 'USOs', or unidentified superconducting objects: reports of extraordinary results that nobody else can reproduce. In 2020 and 2023, the journal Nature published two papers by a group in the United States claiming room-temperature superconductivity in hydrides under pressure; both were later retracted after other scientists raised concerns about the data, and an investigation by the host university found evidence of misconduct. In July 2023, a preprint from South Korea describing a copper-doped lead compound called LK-99 spread rapidly online, with amateur videos appearing to show fragments levitating. Within weeks, laboratories around the world had shown that the partial levitation was caused by ordinary magnetism and that impurities of copper sulphide explained the sudden drop in resistance.

Part of the difficulty is that, outside the conventional BCS framework, there is no reliable theory to tell researchers where to look. Dr Priya Raman, a materials theorist at Imperial College London, compares the situation to 'prospecting for gold without a map of the geology'. Computational methods have improved matters somewhat: by simulating how electrons and lattices interact, researchers can screen thousands of hypothetical compounds before synthesising any. Machine-learning models trained on databases of known superconductors have also been used to propose candidates, although Raman warns that such models tend to suggest variations on materials already known, since they learn from past discoveries. The real breakthroughs, she points out, have usually been accidental: the cuprates were found by people who were not looking for them.

Superconductors are already in everyday use, though always at low temperatures. The magnets inside hospital MRI scanners rely on niobium-titanium wire cooled by liquid helium, and the Large Hadron Collider uses more than a thousand superconducting magnets to steer particles. A material that worked at room temperature and ordinary pressure could, in principle, allow electricity to be transmitted over continental distances with almost no loss, make magnetically levitated trains far cheaper and transform the design of fusion reactors. Some engineers caution, however, that such a material would also need to be cheap, flexible enough to be drawn into wire and able to carry large currents, qualities the cuprates still lack. Even a genuine discovery, in other words, might take decades to reach the power grid.

title: Meat without the animal
sub: Cultivated meat has reached restaurant tables in a handful of countries, but its hardest problems may still lie ahead.

paras.x: In 1931 Winston Churchill predicted that within fifty years humanity would 'escape the absurdity of growing a whole chicken in order to eat the breast or wing'. His timetable proved wildly optimistic. For most of the twentieth century, culturing animal tissue was a laboratory technique used to study disease, not to feed people, and the idea of producing meat this way remained a curiosity for futurists. That changed in 2013, when a hamburger assembled from some 20,000 strips of cow muscle was cooked and tasted in front of journalists in London. The patty had cost roughly a quarter of a million euros to produce, and the tasters judged it dry. Yet the event drew investors, and within a decade more than 150 start-ups had appeared, collectively raising several billion dollars on the promise that the technology was ready to leave the laboratory.

The underlying principle is deceptively simple. A small sample of cells, usually obtained through a painless biopsy from a living animal, is placed in a nutrient-rich liquid known as a growth medium. Certain cells, particularly the satellite cells that repair muscle after injury, can divide repeatedly in these conditions, and a single sample can in theory yield many tonnes of tissue. Once enough cells have accumulated, the chemical signals in the medium are altered so that they stop multiplying and begin to fuse into muscle fibres, or, in separate batches, to store lipids as fat cells. The result, however, is closer to a paste than a cut of meat. To reproduce the grain of a steak, developers must grow the cells on edible scaffolds made from plant proteins or fungal fibres, which provide the support that blood vessels and connective tissue supply in a real animal.

It is the growth medium, rather than the cells themselves, that has proved the most stubborn obstacle. Early experiments relied on fetal bovine serum, a liquid harvested from the blood of unborn calves at slaughter, which sat awkwardly with an industry promising to end animal suffering and cost up to $1,000 a litre. Most companies now claim to have eliminated it, replacing it with recombinant proteins produced by genetically modified bacteria or yeast. These proteins are themselves expensive, however, as they were originally manufactured in tiny quantities for medical research. A 2021 cost model by Dr Imogen Hartley of Wageningen University estimated that the medium accounted for between 55 and 95 per cent of total production costs, and concluded that its price would need to fall by more than 99 per cent before cultivated meat could compete with conventional chicken.

Even if the medium became cheap, scale would remain a formidable challenge. The largest bioreactors used by the pharmaceutical industry hold around 20,000 litres, and a facility capable of supplying a meaningful share of a national meat market would need dozens of far larger vessels. Animal cells are fragile: they are easily damaged by the turbulence needed to mix the liquid, and as tanks grow larger, delivering oxygen evenly without tearing the cells becomes harder. A more insidious risk is contamination. Because cultured cells lack the immune system that protects a living animal, a single bacterium entering the tank can multiply unchecked and ruin a batch worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. Professor Rafael Okonjo, a bioprocess engineer at the University of Nottingham, compares the requirement to 'running an operating theatre the size of a brewery'.

Advocates have long presented cultivated meat as an answer to the climate impact of livestock farming, which by most estimates produces around 14 per cent of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions. Life-cycle assessments, though, paint a more conditional picture. Because bioreactors must be heated, stirred and sterilised continuously, the process is highly energy-intensive, and its footprint depends heavily on how that energy is generated. A 2023 study led by Dr Sunil Varma at the University of California concluded that if the growth medium had to be purified to pharmaceutical standards, the emissions per kilogram could exceed those of beef by a factor of four or more. Supporters responded that food-grade ingredients would make such purification unnecessary, and that a grid powered by renewables would transform the calculation. Both claims remain, for now, largely untested at commercial scale.

Regulators have responded in strikingly different ways. Singapore became the first country to authorise the sale of cultivated meat in December 2020, when chicken bites produced by an American firm went on sale in a single restaurant. The United States followed in 2023 after a joint review by its food and agriculture agencies, and Israel approved a cultivated beef product the following year. Elsewhere, the reaction has been hostile. Italy passed a law in 2023 banning the production and sale of cultivated meat, citing the protection of its culinary heritage, and in 2024 the American states of Florida and Alabama introduced their own prohibitions, despite federal approval. Even where sales are permitted, disputes over labelling persist: producers favour the term 'cultivated', while farming groups argue that consumers should be told plainly that the product was made in a laboratory.

In the end, the technology will succeed or fail on whether people are willing to eat it. Surveys suggest that attitudes are ambivalent rather than settled. A 2022 study of 3,000 consumers in Britain, Germany and Brazil, conducted by Dr Lena Fischbach of the University of Bonn, found that around a third of respondents would try cultivated meat, but fewer than one in ten said they would buy it regularly. Younger and urban respondents were more receptive, while the most common objection was that the product seemed 'unnatural'. Strikingly, the wording of the question made a considerable difference: when the product was described as 'lab-grown', acceptance fell by almost twenty percentage points compared with the phrase 'cultivated meat'. Such findings suggest that public opinion is still malleable, which may explain why producers and their opponents are fighting so hard over vocabulary.

title: Cargoes from the deep
sub: Wrecks on the floor of the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea are changing what historians know about the world's oldest long-distance sea trade.

paras.x: When the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen coined the term 'Silk Road' in 1877, he had in mind the caravan routes that crossed the deserts and mountains of Central Asia. The phrase has shaped popular imagination ever since, conjuring images of camel trains and oasis cities. Yet for much of the past two millennia, the bulk of trade between East and West moved not overland but by sea. A single large merchant vessel could carry as much cargo as several hundred camels, and it could do so without paying tolls to the rulers of every territory it passed through. Historians have increasingly argued that the sea lanes linking China, South-East Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa deserve to be regarded as the more important of the two systems, even if they have received a fraction of the scholarly attention.

The engine of this maritime network was the monsoon. In the Indian Ocean, prevailing winds blow from the south-west between roughly June and September and reverse direction in the winter months, a pattern that sailors learned to exploit at least two thousand years ago. A merchant leaving the Persian Gulf in late autumn could reach the west coast of India within weeks, but would then have to wait several months for the winds to change before continuing or returning. These enforced pauses had consequences that extended far beyond navigation. Traders settled for long periods in ports such as Calicut, Malacca and Quanzhou, marrying locally, building places of worship and forming communities that acted as intermediaries for later arrivals. According to Dr Amara Weerasinghe of the University of Peradeniya, many of the region's mixed coastal cultures can be traced directly to this seasonal waiting.

Much of what is now known about the scale of this commerce comes from shipwrecks. In 1998, fishermen diving for sea cucumbers off the Indonesian island of Belitung discovered the remains of a ninth-century vessel whose planks had been stitched together with coconut fibre rather than fastened with nails, a technique characteristic of boats built in Arabia or the Persian Gulf. On board were around 60,000 ceramic objects, the great majority of them bowls from the Changsha kilns in southern China. Many were decorated with lotus patterns, Arabic inscriptions and geometric designs evidently intended to appeal to customers in western Asia. One bowl bears a date corresponding to the year 826. For historians, the significance lay less in any individual piece than in the evidence of standardised production: Chinese workshops were clearly making goods in vast quantities for consumers they would never meet.

A second landmark find required a quite different approach. The Nanhai No. 1, a merchant ship of the Song dynasty that sank in the twelfth or thirteenth century, was located off the southern coast of China in 1987. Rather than excavating it piece by piece on the sea floor, where visibility was poor and silt constantly shifted, Chinese archaeologists decided in 2007 to lift the entire wreck, together with the surrounding sediment, inside a vast steel container weighing, with its contents, more than 5,000 tonnes. The container was then moved into a purpose-built museum, where it sits in a pool of water kept at the same temperature and chemical composition as the seabed. Excavation has proceeded slowly in full view of visitors, and more than 180,000 objects have been recovered, including porcelain, iron goods, coins and gold jewellery.

Beyond the cargo itself, the personal possessions of crews reveal who was actually doing the trading. On several wrecks, archaeologists have found cooking pots from one region, gaming pieces from another and religious objects from a third, suggesting that crews were drawn from many different communities. Dr Tomasz Wierzbicki of the University of Oxford, who catalogued the domestic items from four wrecks in the Java Sea, argues that the typical vessel 'was built in one place, sailed by men from another and loaded with goods from a third'. What emerges is a system that operated without any single state in charge. Unlike the European trading companies that arrived in the sixteenth century, backed by armed fleets and seeking monopolies, earlier merchants generally depended on negotiation, shared customs and a degree of mutual trust.

The value of such discoveries has also made them targets. The Belitung cargo was recovered not by a research institute but by a commercial salvage company, which later sold the collection to the government of Singapore for a reported 32 million dollars. When an exhibition of the material was planned at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington in 2011, archaeologists protested that displaying it would legitimise the practice of excavating sites for profit, and the museum postponed the show indefinitely. Defenders of the salvage operation pointed out that the wreck lay in shallow water, was already being looted by local divers, and might otherwise have been lost entirely. The episode exposed a deep divide between those who see a wreck chiefly as a source of objects and those who regard it as a scientific context whose value is destroyed once items are removed without careful recording. A 2001 UNESCO convention attempts to restrict commercial exploitation, but many coastal states have yet to ratify it.

Newer scientific techniques are now extracting information that earlier excavators could not have imagined. Chemical analysis of residues inside storage jars can identify their original contents, while isotope studies of timber and ceramics can pinpoint where they were produced. Yet researchers are increasingly conscious of the limits of the evidence. Shipwrecks represent only the voyages that failed, and they may over-represent particular routes, such as those through treacherous straits, where ships were most likely to sink. Equally, the materials that survive centuries underwater are mostly ceramics, metal and stone. Silk, spices and other organic goods, which may well have accounted for most of the value traded, rarely leave any trace. As Dr Weerasinghe observes, the Maritime Silk Road reconstructed from the seabed is, somewhat paradoxically, one in which silk is almost entirely absent.

title: The self-healing secret of Roman concrete
sub: Why do structures built two thousand years ago outlast many modern ones? Scientists believe they are finally beginning to understand.

paras.x: Nearly nineteen centuries after it was completed, the dome of the Pantheon in Rome remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Elsewhere across the former empire, Roman harbour walls, aqueducts and bridges have endured earthquakes, floods and centuries of neglect. Modern concrete, by contrast, often begins to crack and crumble within fifty to a hundred years, and the cost of repairing deteriorating bridges, tunnels and car parks runs to billions of pounds a year in Britain alone. The contrast has long puzzled engineers. For much of the twentieth century it was assumed that the Romans had simply been fortunate, or that only their best work had survived while inferior structures had vanished. Over the past two decades, however, laboratory research has suggested that the material itself possessed properties that its modern successor lacks.

The basic ingredients were described by the architect Vitruvius in the first century BC. Roman builders combined lime, made by heating limestone, with volcanic ash and fragments of rock or brick known as aggregate. The most prized ash came from around the town of Pozzuoli, near Naples, and was so valued that it was shipped to construction sites as far away as Caesarea in present-day Israel. When the ash is mixed with lime and water, its silica and alumina react to form compounds that bind the mixture together, a process now termed the pozzolanic reaction after the town itself. The resulting material was not especially strong in compression, but it was unusually resistant to the gradual chemical attack that weakens most cements over time.

The most baffling case concerned structures built in the sea. Roman writers claimed that harbour concrete became stronger with each passing year, a statement modern scientists initially dismissed as exaggeration. Seawater, after all, is notoriously destructive to modern concrete. Yet when Dr Clara Benedetti of the University of Utah examined cores drilled from ancient piers in the Bay of Naples in 2017, she found that seawater percolating through the material had dissolved parts of the volcanic ash and allowed new minerals to crystallise in the gaps. Among these were rare crystals of aluminous tobermorite, which are extremely difficult to produce in a modern laboratory without very high temperatures. These interlocking crystals appear to have reinforced the concrete from within, so that the very environment expected to destroy it had, in effect, made it more cohesive.

Marine structures, however, are only part of the story, since Roman concrete on land has also proved remarkably durable. Here attention has turned to tiny white lumps of lime, usually only a few millimetres across, that are scattered through almost every sample. For decades these 'lime clasts' were regarded as evidence of careless mixing or poor-quality raw materials. In 2023, a team led by Professor Daniel Reyes at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology proposed a radically different interpretation. Their analysis suggested that the Romans had not used slaked lime, as was generally believed, but quicklime, a highly reactive form that generates intense heat when it meets water. This 'hot mixing' would leave behind brittle, calcium-rich clasts, which could serve as a reservoir of material ready to repair the concrete when needed.

The mechanism is straightforward in principle. When a crack forms, it tends to pass through the clasts, which are weaker than the surrounding material. If water then enters the crack, it dissolves calcium from the clast, and the resulting solution either reacts with carbon dioxide to form calcium carbonate or combines with the volcanic ash, sealing the fracture. To test the idea, the MIT team produced samples using both ancient and modern methods, deliberately cracked them and passed water through the gaps. Within two weeks, the cracks in the hot-mixed samples had closed completely and water could no longer flow, whereas the samples made without quicklime remained permeable. The researchers also observed that hot mixing allowed the material to set considerably faster, which may help to explain how the Romans built so quickly.

Admirers of Roman engineering sometimes ask why builders do not simply return to the ancient recipe. The answer is that the two materials were designed for different purposes. Roman concrete is relatively weak under compression and was never combined with internal steel bars, so it could not support the slender beams and tall towers that modern cities require. Ironically, the steel reinforcement that makes modern concrete so adaptable is also one of its main weaknesses: when water and salt penetrate, the steel corrodes and expands, splitting the surrounding concrete apart. Roman structures avoided this problem largely because they contained no metal to rust. Dr Fiona McAllister, a structural engineer at Imperial College London, cautions that 'durability and performance are trade-offs, and the Romans optimised for one at the expense of the other'.

Even so, the ancient material may offer lessons that are increasingly relevant. The production of Portland cement, the main ingredient of modern concrete, is responsible for roughly eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, largely because limestone must be heated to around 1,450 degrees Celsius. Replacing part of the cement with volcanic ash or similar materials lowers both the energy required and the emissions released, and structures that repair themselves would need replacing less often. Several start-up companies are now experimenting with self-healing mixes inspired by the MIT findings, and some engineers see particular promise in sea walls built to withstand rising sea levels. Caution is still warranted, though. A concrete designed to last two thousand years cannot be tested over that period, and accelerated laboratory trials may not capture how materials behave in real conditions over centuries.

title: The Uses of Tedium
sub: Long dismissed as a trivial complaint, boredom is now taken seriously by psychologists, though they disagree about what it is for.

paras.x: For an experience that almost everyone recognises, boredom has had a surprisingly short career as an object of study. The English noun itself is relatively young: it appears to have entered general use only in the 1850s, when Charles Dickens gave it to the chronically weary Lady Dedlock in Bleak House. Philosophers from Schopenhauer to Heidegger wrote at length about the condition, yet experimental psychologists largely left it alone. A bibliometric survey published in 2021 by Dr Imogen Hartley of the University of Exeter counted fewer than forty empirical papers on boredom before 1980, compared with more than six hundred in the single decade to 2020. Hartley attributes the change less to any single discovery than to a growing suspicion that boredom is linked to problems which do attract funding, from school dropout to gambling.

The most influential explanation to emerge from this surge is functional. On this account, boredom is not a mere absence of feeling but an emotion with a job to do: it signals that the current activity has stopped delivering anything of value and pushes the person to look elsewhere. Professor Tomas Lindqvist of Uppsala University compares it to physical pain, arguing that the unpleasantness is precisely the point, since a signal that felt neutral would be easy to ignore. Supporters of the view often cite a 2014 American experiment in which volunteers were left alone in a bare room for fifteen minutes with nothing but a button that delivered a mild electric shock. Around two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women pressed it at least once, having earlier said they would pay to avoid the sensation. For Lindqvist, this shows how strongly the mind resists an empty interval.

Yet if boredom is to be studied, it must first be measured, and here the field has struggled. For three decades the standard instrument was the Boredom Proneness Scale, a questionnaire developed in 1986 which asks people to agree or disagree with statements such as 'Time always seems to be passing slowly'. Critics have pointed out that the scale captures a stable disposition rather than the feeling itself, and that several of its items correlate so closely with measures of depression and poor attention that it is unclear what is left once these are removed. Newer approaches treat boredom as a passing state, using smartphone apps that prompt participants at random moments during the day, a method that, according to Dr Priya Raman of the University of Toronto, reveals that people report being bored for roughly a fifth of their waking hours, far more than they estimate in retrospect.

Laboratory studies face a different difficulty: boredom has to be produced on demand. The tasks devised for this purpose are deliberately dreary. Participants have been asked to copy numbers from a telephone directory, to turn pegs a quarter-turn for half an hour, or to watch a video in which two men hang washing on a line without speaking. Such procedures reliably lower self-reported interest, but sceptics question what else they produce. Dr Samuel Okafor, who studies emotion at the University of Bristol, notes that people subjected to these tasks also report frustration, irritation and, in some cases, resentment towards the experimenter. 'There is also the matter of context,' he says. 'A student who knows the session ends in twenty minutes and earns course credit is not in the same position as a factory worker facing another eight hours.' Laboratory boredom, in other words, may be a pale and contaminated copy of the real thing.

Nowhere have these methodological doubts mattered more than in research on creativity. In a study that attracted wide press coverage, Dr Rachel Ainsworth of Lancaster University asked one group of volunteers to spend fifteen minutes copying telephone numbers, while a control group went straight to the main task: thinking of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had endured the tedious copying produced significantly more ideas. Ainsworth proposed that boredom encourages the mind to wander, and that a wandering mind makes unusual connections. The finding was quickly translated into advice. Newspaper columns urged parents to stop entertaining their children during school holidays, and at least one management consultancy began recommending 'unstructured time' for staff, citing the study as its evidence base.

More recent work has been less obliging. In 2019, a consortium coordinated by Dr Hyun-woo Park of Seoul National University repeated Ainsworth's procedure in laboratories in five countries, with a combined sample several times larger than the original. The effect appeared at only two sites, and when the data were pooled it was too small to be distinguished from chance. Park's team also drew attention to a problem of scoring. The cups task is usually marked for fluency, the sheer number of responses, and for originality, judged by independent raters. Bored participants, it seems, may write more simply because any activity is a relief after copying numbers; the originality of their ideas was no higher than that of controls. A meta-analysis published two years later reached a similar conclusion: boredom predicts quantity, but there is little evidence that it predicts quality.

None of this means that boredom is useless, only that its benefits may be indirect and unreliable. If the functional account is correct, boredom launches a search for something more rewarding, but it does not dictate what that something will be. The same restlessness that sends one person to a sketchbook sends another to the biscuit tin, the betting app or a dangerous drive. Lindqvist suspects that smartphones have altered the equation by offering instant relief, so that the signal is silenced before it can prompt any deliberate change of course. 'The interesting question,' he says, 'is not whether boredom is good for us, but what we do in the minutes after it arrives.' Several groups are now attempting to answer exactly that, tracking participants' behaviour in the period immediately following a reported episode of boredom.

title: Remembering What Never Happened
sub: Memory feels like a recording, but decades of experiments suggest it is closer to a reconstruction, with uncomfortable consequences for the courtroom.

paras.x: Ask people how memory works and many will describe something like a video camera. In a 2018 poll of 2,000 British adults, commissioned by the Centre for Legal Psychology in Leicester, 58 per cent agreed that memories, once formed, remain fixed and can in principle be replayed accurately, while almost half believed that hypnosis could recover events that had been forgotten. The appeal of the metaphor is easy to understand: remembering feels like seeing, and vivid recollections arrive with a sense of certainty that seems to guarantee their accuracy. Psychologists have been arguing against this picture for nearly a century, but with limited success outside their own discipline. That matters, because jurors bring the same assumptions into court, and a witness who remembers in confident, vivid detail is far more likely to be believed than one who hesitates.

The case against the recording model was first set out by Frederic Bartlett at Cambridge in the early 1930s. Bartlett asked English students to read a Native American folk tale, 'The War of the Ghosts', and then to reproduce it from memory at intervals of days, weeks and in a few cases years. With each retelling, the story became shorter and more conventional. Unfamiliar details, such as the supernatural elements, were dropped or rationalised, and the narrative drifted towards the kind of story his participants already knew. Bartlett concluded that remembering is not the retrieval of a stored copy but an act of construction, in which fragments of the original experience are combined with general knowledge, which he called 'schemas', about how such events usually unfold. The gaps are filled in automatically, and the person doing the remembering is generally unaware that this has happened.

For several decades Bartlett's ideas were treated as suggestive rather than proven, partly because his methods were informal by modern standards. The decisive shift came in the 1970s, when Elizabeth Loftus and her colleagues in the United States showed that memory could be altered by the wording of a single question. Students watched film of a traffic accident and were then asked how fast the cars were going when they 'hit' or 'smashed into' each other. Those given the more violent verb estimated higher speeds, and a week later they were more than twice as likely to report having seen broken glass, although none had appeared in the film. This 'misinformation effect' has since been reproduced hundreds of times. Its practical message is uncomfortable: an investigator need not intend to mislead in order to change what a witness later recalls.

Changing a detail is one thing; creating an entire event is another. In the 1990s, researchers began trying to persuade adults that they had experienced things in childhood which their families confirmed had never happened, such as being lost in a shopping centre. Roughly a quarter of participants came to accept the invented episode, sometimes elaborating on it with sensory details of their own. Later studies used doctored photographs showing participants as children in the basket of a hot-air balloon, with similar or higher success rates. The most striking claim came in 2015, when a Canadian study reported that 70 per cent of students could be led, over three interviews, to recall committing a crime as teenagers, in some cases an assault. The figure was widely reported, and for a time it was quoted as evidence that almost anyone can be made to confess to anything.

That conclusion now looks premature. Much depends on how a 'false memory' is defined and counted. Dr Marta Esteves of the University of Lisbon points out that early studies often coded a participant as having a false memory if they merely accepted that an event might have occurred and offered some imagined detail. 'Believing that something probably happened is not the same as remembering it,' she says. When Esteves and her colleagues reanalysed the transcripts of eight implantation studies using stricter criteria, requiring participants to describe the event as a personal experience, with a sense of reliving it, the average rate fell to around 30 per cent, and in the crime study to well under half the published figure. Esteves does not dispute that false memories can be produced; she questions whether the most dramatic figures tell us much about what happens outside a research setting.

Whatever the precise rates, the courtroom implications have been taken seriously. Analyses of convictions in the United States later overturned through DNA evidence have found that mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in around seven in ten cases. Many of these errors appear to have been shaped by procedure rather than by any defect in the witness. A witness who picks someone from a line-up and is then told 'Good, you identified our suspect' typically becomes more confident over the following months, and it is this inflated confidence that a jury eventually sees. In response, a number of police forces have introduced line-ups run by an officer who does not know which person is the suspect, and require that a witness's level of certainty be written down at the moment of the first identification, before any feedback can contaminate it.

Some researchers now warn that the pendulum may swing too far. Professor Alan Whitcombe of Durham University argues that the false-memory literature, by concentrating on spectacular failures, has encouraged a belief that memory is hopelessly unreliable, which is no more accurate than the video-camera model it replaced. Most memories, he notes, are broadly correct about the core of an event even when peripheral details are wrong, and an initial identification made confidently under fair conditions is a reasonably good indicator of accuracy. His concern is that defence lawyers can use the research to cast doubt on any witness, including victims whose testimony is genuine. The more defensible position, he suggests, is to treat memory as a form of trace evidence: valuable, but easily contaminated, and only as trustworthy as the procedures used to collect it.

title: Second Thoughts About the Second Brain
sub: The idea that gut bacteria shape our moods has captured the public imagination. The evidence is more interesting, and more limited, than the headlines suggest.

paras.x: Few areas of biology have moved so quickly from the laboratory into the supermarket. A decade ago the phrase 'gut-brain axis' was largely confined to specialist journals; today it appears on the labels of yoghurts, kombucha and capsules promising calmer moods and sharper thinking. Probiotic supplements marketed specifically for mental well-being, sometimes described as 'psychobiotics', now form a distinct product category, and one industry estimate valued global sales at around 1.5 billion dollars in 2024. Popular books describe the intestine as a 'second brain' and suggest that anxiety or low mood may begin with an imbalance of microbes. The scientific literature has grown almost as fast as the market, with several thousand papers a year now mentioning the microbiome in connection with the nervous system. Yet researchers in the field are often notably more cautious than the products that cite their work.

There are good reasons to think that gut microbes could, in principle, influence the brain. The intestine is connected to the brainstem by the vagus nerve, which carries signals in both directions, and bacteria produce a range of chemicals, among them short-chain fatty acids formed when they digest fibre, which enter the bloodstream and affect inflammation throughout the body. The case of serotonin is often mentioned. Around 90 per cent of the body's serotonin, a chemical messenger associated with mood, is made in the gut, and microbes help to regulate its production. What is mentioned less often is that serotonin produced in the intestine does not cross from the blood into the brain, which manufactures its own supply. The existence of plausible pathways, in other words, establishes that a connection is possible; it does not show how important that connection is.

The most persuasive evidence so far comes from animals. In an influential experiment published in 2004, a team in Japan raised mice in sterile isolators so that they had no gut bacteria at all. When briefly restrained, these 'germ-free' animals released considerably more stress hormone than ordinary mice, and the exaggerated response could be partly reversed by giving them a particular bacterium, but only if this was done at a young age. Subsequent work has shown that transferring the gut contents of one mouse strain into another can shift behaviour: timid animals become more exploratory, or the reverse. In 2016, researchers in Ireland went a step further, transplanting faecal samples from people with depression into rats whose own microbes had been depleted with antibiotics. The rats became less interested in sweetened water, a change usually interpreted as a sign of depression-like behaviour.

How far such findings apply to people is a matter of active dispute. Dr Helen Achterberg, a neuroscientist at Leiden University, points out that germ-free mice are a profoundly artificial creation: their immune systems and even the structure of their intestines develop abnormally, so differences between them and normal animals may reveal little about the modest variations found among healthy humans. The behavioural tests are also open to question. A rat drinking less sugar solution, or a mouse that stops swimming sooner when placed in a tank of water, may be displaying something quite unlike human depression. 'We are not measuring sadness,' Achterberg says. 'We are measuring a behaviour and agreeing to call it something.' She adds that laboratory rodents, fed uniform diets in clean cages, host microbial communities that bear little resemblance to those of people living ordinary lives.

Human studies are fewer, and most of them are observational. In 2019, an analysis of more than a thousand participants in Belgium found that two groups of bacteria were consistently scarcer in people who reported depression, even after allowing for antidepressant use, and the result was confirmed in a separate Dutch sample. Such studies identify associations, but the direction of cause is very hard to establish. Depression typically alters appetite, sleep and physical activity, all of which reshape the microbiome, and many medicines, not only antidepressants, have effects on gut bacteria. Dr Owen Gallagher of University College Cork describes the problem bluntly: 'If people who are depressed eat differently, their bacteria will be different. That tells you depression changes the gut. It does not tell you the gut causes depression.' Only following people over many years, he argues, could begin to separate the two.

The obvious way to test causation is to change the microbiome and see what happens to mood, and dozens of trials have attempted this using probiotics. The results are, at best, mixed. A 2022 review led by Dr Fatima Rahman of King's College London pooled 34 trials and found a small benefit among people with a clinical diagnosis of depression, usually when the probiotic was taken alongside conventional treatment, but no detectable effect in healthy volunteers, who are the main customers for mood supplements. Rahman also noted that most trials lasted fewer than twelve weeks, enrolled fewer than a hundred participants and used different bacterial strains, making it difficult to say which product, if any, was responsible. Around a third were funded by manufacturers, and those trials reported positive findings more often than independently funded ones.

None of this means that the gut-brain connection is imaginary. Most researchers in the field believe it is real and potentially important, and some expect that particular microbial products may one day be used to support treatment for certain patients. The difficulty lies in the distance between that cautious expectation and the confident claims of marketing and media coverage, where results in mice are routinely presented as though they applied to people, and associations are reported as causes. Achterberg suggests that the field has partly brought this on itself, through press releases that emphasise the most dramatic animal results. What is needed now, she argues, is less excitement and more patience: long-term studies following people before and after they become unwell, and trials designed to test specific mechanisms rather than general claims about well-being.

title: The Enemy of Our Enemy
sub: As antibiotics lose their power, doctors are returning to a century-old treatment that uses viruses to hunt bacteria

paras.x: When Alexander Fleming accepted his Nobel Prize in 1945, he used part of his lecture to issue a warning: a patient who took too little penicillin, he suggested, might end up educating the microbes rather than killing them. For several decades the caution was largely ignored, partly because new classes of antibiotic kept arriving fast enough to replace those that failed. That cushion has now gone. A study coordinated by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation in Seattle estimated that in 2019 roughly 1.27 million deaths were directly caused by bacteria that no longer responded to standard drugs, more than were attributed to HIV or malaria that year. The routine use of antibiotics to speed the growth of livestock, still permitted in many countries, has made matters worse, as has the casual prescription of the drugs for viral illnesses on which they have no effect whatsoever.

One might expect the pharmaceutical industry to rush into the gap, yet the opposite has happened. Of the eighteen largest drug companies active in the field in the 1990s, only a handful still run antibiotic research programmes. The reasoning is grimly commercial. A new cancer medicine may be taken for months or years and can command a high price; a new antibiotic is typically prescribed for a week, and, if it is genuinely novel, doctors are urged to hold it in reserve for the most desperate cases so that resistance to it does not develop. 'You end up with a product that everyone agrees is valuable and nobody is allowed to buy,' says Dr Miriam Okafor, a health economist at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. Several small firms that did bring antibiotics to market in the last decade have since filed for bankruptcy.

It is against this background that an older idea has been rediscovered. In 1917 the French-Canadian microbiologist Félix d'Herelle described an 'invisible microbe' that destroyed dysentery bacteria, and named it a bacteriophage, literally a 'bacteria eater'. (The English scientist Frederick Twort had observed something similar two years earlier, and the question of priority was argued over for decades.) D'Herelle went on to treat patients with phage preparations in Paris and India, and by the 1930s commercial phage products were on sale in Europe and the United States. Yet when penicillin became widely available after the Second World War, Western medicine dropped phages almost entirely. Only in the Soviet Union, and above all at the Eliava Institute in Tbilisi, Georgia, did the research continue, and it is to Tbilisi that desperate patients from abroad still travel today.

Phages possess several characteristics that make them attractive to clinicians. Each type infects only a narrow range of bacterial strains, so, unlike broad-spectrum antibiotics, they leave the beneficial microbes of the gut and skin unharmed. They also multiply at the site of infection: a phage injects its genetic material into a bacterial cell, hijacks the cell's machinery to manufacture perhaps a hundred copies of itself, and then bursts the cell open, releasing the new particles to attack neighbouring bacteria. In principle, therefore, the dose increases precisely where it is needed and declines once its hosts are exhausted. Phages are also extraordinarily abundant, being the most numerous biological entities on the planet, and suitable candidates can often be isolated from sewage within days.

For decades such advantages remained theoretical in the West, but a series of individual cases has changed the mood. In 2016 Professor Daniel Ashworth, a psychologist at a Californian university, fell into a coma after contracting a multidrug-resistant infection while on holiday in Egypt. With conventional options exhausted, his wife, an epidemiologist, contacted phage researchers across the world, and an intravenous cocktail assembled from samples in Texas and Maryland was administered under emergency rules. Within days he regained consciousness. Similar stories followed, including that of a teenage girl in London with cystic fibrosis whose treatment used a genetically modified virus. Researchers are careful to point out that anecdotes are not evidence; such patients were often receiving antibiotics simultaneously, which makes it hard to know which intervention was responsible.

Turning such successes into routine medicine is proving difficult. Drug regulators are designed to evaluate a single, fixed product that can be manufactured identically for every patient. Phage therapy, by contrast, often works best when a cocktail is matched to the particular strain infecting an individual and adjusted as the infection evolves. 'The regulatory system assumes the medicine stays still,' notes Dr Lena Brandt of the Charité hospital in Berlin. 'Ours is designed to change.' The few large randomised trials conducted so far have been disappointing: one European study of phages for burn wound infections was halted early after the phage preparation proved far less concentrated than intended, and the treated patients fared worse than those on standard care. Patent law presents a further complication, since naturally occurring viruses cannot easily be owned, which discourages private investment.

Perhaps the most promising avenue lies not in replacing antibiotics but in combining the two approaches. Bacteria do evolve resistance to phages, frequently by altering or discarding the surface structures the viruses use to attach themselves. Researchers at Yale University have shown that in some species these same structures act as pumps that expel antibiotics from the cell. A bacterium that sheds them to escape a phage may therefore become vulnerable once more to drugs it had previously shrugged off. Whether this evolutionary trade-off can be exploited reliably in hospitals remains contested, and sceptics warn that enthusiasm has outrun the data before. Even so, few microbiologists now dismiss phages as a historical curiosity.

title: Less Is More?
sub: Pilot schemes suggest a shorter working week need not cost employers, but economists disagree about what the evidence really shows

paras.x: In 1930 the economist John Maynard Keynes published a short essay in which he predicted that, within a century, rising productivity would allow his grandchildren to work perhaps fifteen hours a week. The forecast looked plausible at the time. Working hours in industrialised countries had fallen steeply since the mid-nineteenth century, when a seventy-hour week was unremarkable, and in 1926 the carmaker Henry Ford had adopted a five-day week in his factories, reasoning that workers with free time would buy more consumer goods, including his cars. Yet after the Second World War the decline slowed dramatically. In most rich economies average annual hours have fallen only modestly since the 1980s, and in some professions they have actually risen, as gains in output were taken as higher incomes rather than as additional leisure.

The idea of a further reduction has returned largely through a series of organised pilots. Between 2015 and 2019 roughly 2,500 public employees in Iceland, around one per cent of the working population, moved to a week of 35 or 36 hours without any loss of pay, and trade unions subsequently negotiated similar terms for most of the country's workforce. In 2022 the campaign group 4 Day Week Global coordinated a six-month trial in Britain involving 61 organisations and nearly 3,000 staff. It was based on a principle of 100 per cent pay for 80 per cent of the time, in exchange for a commitment to maintain 100 per cent of output. At the end, 56 of the participating firms chose to continue, and revenue across the sample was broadly unchanged, rising marginally in some cases.

Advocates argue that such results are less surprising than they appear. Much of the conventional working week, they contend, is occupied by tasks of doubtful value: meetings that run on too long, emails that need not be sent, and the general drift that occurs when work expands to fill the time available. When the week is shortened, staff tend to scrutinise these habits ruthlessly. Dr Aoife Brennan, an organisational psychologist at University College Dublin, found that firms in an Irish trial reduced the average length of internal meetings by almost a third. Rested employees are also less likely to fall ill; sick days in the British pilot fell by around two thirds, and resignations dropped sharply, which spared employers the considerable expense of recruiting and training replacements.

Sceptics, however, point to weaknesses in how the evidence was gathered. Every firm in the British pilot volunteered to take part, and companies confident that a shorter week would suit them are hardly a random sample of the economy. Much of the data on well-being came from staff surveys, and employees who value an extra day off have an obvious incentive to report that the arrangement is working. Measuring productivity is itself problematic outside manufacturing: in a design studio or a law firm, output is not easily counted. 'Revenue staying flat over six months tells you surprisingly little,' argues Professor Hugo Lindqvist, a labour economist at Stockholm University. 'You need years of data, and a comparison group that did not change anything, before drawing firm conclusions.'

Even enthusiasts concede that the model is far easier to introduce in some industries than in others. An accountancy firm can close on Fridays; a hospital, a care home or a supermarket cannot, because staff must be physically present whenever patients or customers are. In such settings a shorter week generally requires hiring additional workers, which raises costs directly, at least in the short term. Some employers have responded by squeezing the same number of hours into four longer days instead. This version keeps opening times intact but carries its own risks: a study of nurses in Ontario working ten-hour shifts found error rates rising noticeably in the final two hours. Lower-paid staff who rely on overtime payments have also been wary of schemes that might reduce their earnings.

Governments have approached the issue in strikingly different ways. In 2022 Belgium gave employees the legal right to request a four-day week, though without any reduction in total hours, so that the change is essentially one of scheduling. Spain, by contrast, set aside around ten million euros to subsidise small firms willing to cut hours while keeping wages stable. In Japan, where long working hours have been linked to deaths from overwork, the government has encouraged employers to offer a third day off each week, partly in the hope that workers will use it to marry and raise children. Unions in several countries are pressing for legislation, but most ministries remain cautious, fearing that a mandatory change could damage competitiveness in export-oriented sectors.

The most important unanswered question may be whether the benefits endure. Industrial psychologists have long known that workers often perform better simply because they are being studied, a phenomenon first associated with experiments at the Hawthorne plant near Chicago in the 1920s. Early follow-up data are mildly encouraging: a year after the British trial ended, most firms were still operating a shorter week, and few reported a decline in performance. But the Swedish city of Gothenburg abandoned a trial of six-hour days for care workers in 2017, concluding that the extra staff it required were too expensive. The likeliest outcome, Lindqvist suggests, is not a universal shift but a gradual spread among office-based firms competing for skilled employees.

title: The Last Speakers
sub: Thousands of the world's languages may fall silent this century, yet a handful of revivals suggest that decline is not inevitable

paras.x: Estimating how quickly the world's languages are disappearing is surprisingly difficult. Linguists broadly accept that around 7,000 are currently spoken, but many have never been properly surveyed, and the boundary between a language and a dialect is often drawn on political rather than linguistic grounds. A figure frequently repeated in the press, that one language dies every fortnight, has been dismissed by Dr Tomás Ferreira of the University of Lisbon as 'more slogan than statistic'. What is not disputed is that speakers are spread very unevenly: fewer than twenty-five languages are the mother tongues of over half the global population. And even cautious projections, such as one published in 2022 by a team at the Australian National University, suggest that without intervention at least 1,500 languages could cease to be spoken by the end of this century.

Languages seldom die because every speaker perishes at once, though epidemics and massacres have occasionally caused exactly that. Far more often, the process is one of shift: a community gradually adopts a more powerful language for school, trade and government, and parents, hoping to improve their children's prospects, stop speaking the ancestral tongue at home. Once a single generation grows up without it, recovery becomes very difficult. Stigma has frequently accelerated the change. In parts of Wales, Australia and North America, children were once physically punished for using their first language in the classroom, and many grew up associating it with poverty or backwardness. Urban migration has a similar effect, since young people who move to cities in search of work typically marry outside their linguistic group.

What is lost when a language falls silent is a matter of some debate. The most obvious casualty is a body of oral literature, songs and histories that may never have been written down. But researchers also emphasise less visible kinds of knowledge. Dr Rosalind Haigh, an ethnobotanist at the University of Auckland, has documented Pacific languages with names for dozens of local plant varieties that Western botanists only recognised as distinct species decades later. Some languages also possess grammatical structures that challenge assumptions about human cognition; several in South America, for instance, require speakers to indicate in the verb itself whether they witnessed an event or merely heard about it. Each loss narrows the evidence on which general theories of language are built.

Revival is possible, but the most celebrated example is also the most unusual. By the late nineteenth century Hebrew had not been anyone's native language for nearly two thousand years, although it survived in prayer, scholarship and writing. Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, who settled in Jerusalem in 1881, insisted on speaking only Hebrew to his family and compiled a dictionary that coined words for modern objects. Within a few decades thousands of children were acquiring it as their first language. Scholars caution, however, that the circumstances were exceptional: immigrants from dozens of countries needed a shared language, a large written tradition already existed, and the revival was bound up with a powerful political movement. Few endangered languages today enjoy any of these advantages.

Other successes have been more modest but perhaps more instructive. In New Zealand, where by the 1970s fewer than one in five Māori people could speak their language fluently, community leaders established the first kōhanga reo, or 'language nests', in 1982. These pre-schools, run largely by grandparents, immersed infants entirely in Māori, and a parallel system of primary and secondary schools followed. In Wales, similar immersion education, supported by a Welsh-language television channel launched in 1982 and by legislation giving the language official status, has helped stabilise the number of speakers. The lesson most linguists draw is that formal lessons for adults rarely produce fluent speakers; transmission to young children is what counts.

Technology plays an ambiguous role. Inexpensive recording equipment has transformed documentation, and a speaker's knowledge can now be archived in hours rather than transcribed laboriously over months. Smartphone applications allow learners in scattered communities to practise vocabulary, and some groups have worked with engineers to build speech-recognition and predictive-text tools for their languages. Yet the internet itself is overwhelmingly dominated by a few major languages, and voice assistants and translation software can deepen the sense that a small language is irrelevant to modern life. Communities have also become uneasy about who owns the recordings made of their elders. One Māori broadcaster in New Zealand, for example, declined offers from large technology firms to purchase its Māori speech data, arguing that it should remain under Indigenous control.

Perhaps the most significant change in the field concerns how success is defined. Earlier generations of linguists tended to judge a revival by whether it produced native speakers in large numbers, a standard few projects could meet. Today many favour a broader view. The Myaamia language of the American Midwest had no living speakers by the 1960s, yet using missionary records and early dictionaries, members of the Miami Tribe have reintroduced it in homes and summer camps, and a small number of children now use it daily. Researchers in Canada have also reported that Indigenous communities where more members know their ancestral language tend to show better health outcomes among young people. If such findings hold, the value of a revival may lie as much in identity and well-being as in numbers.
